country.name: Russia
country.tagline: Imperial sparkling at Abrau-Durso, the Don Cossacks' native reds and a protected, fast-growing domestic industry.

stats.note: OIV 2025 (figures as reported by Russia, including occupied Crimea and Sevastopol, which are internationally recognised as Ukraine).

country.overview:
Most of Russia is too cold for vines, but its south, along the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and the Caspian, has a wine history as old as anyone's. Greek colonies on the Taman peninsula (Phanagoria, Gorgippia at today's Anapa) made wine in the sixth century BC. The Don Cossacks grew vines on the river's islands and terraces from the seventeenth century and kept their own red grapes, Tsimlyansky Cherny, Krasnostop Zolotovsky and Plechistik; the sparkling red Tsimlyanskoye was praised by Pushkin.

In 1870 Tsar Alexander II founded an imperial estate at Abrau-Durso, by a mountain lake near Novorossiysk, and in 1891 Prince Lev Golitsyn, already famous for Crimea's Novy Svet, took charge and brought French specialists to make sparkling wine by the traditional method. The Soviet Union turned Abrau-Durso into the model for 'Sovetskoye Shampanskoye', most of which was made by the tank method in giant plants. Gorbachev's 1985 campaign destroyed much of the vineyard.

Since the 2000s private investment has rebuilt Kuban (Krasnodar Krai), now the heart of Russian wine, with the Taman peninsula, Anapa and the Krymsk-Abrau area: Fanagoria, Kuban-Vino (Château Tamagne), Lefkadia, Gai-Kodzor, Château le Grand Vostock, Abrau-Durso (now a listed company and Russia's largest sparkling wine producer) and many small estates. The Don valley in Rostov oblast, Stavropol and Dagestan (Derbent) add native grapes and brandy. A federal law on viticulture and winemaking in force from June 2020 reserved 'Russian wine' for wine from Russian grapes and set up protected geographical indications (ZGU) and protected designations of origin (ZNMP). Approved geographical names include Kuban, Kuban. Taman Peninsula, Don Valley, Stavropol, Dagestan, Terek Valley, Lower Volga and Crimea; by 2020 there were 15 ZGU and 23 ZNMP, with more since. Import duties on wine from countries Russia designates 'unfriendly' rose to 20 percent in 2023 and 25 percent in 2024, handing domestic producers a protected market. Production reached 5.7 million hectolitres in 2025.

history.title: Phanagoria and Gorgippia
history.text: Greek colonists on the Taman peninsula and at Gorgippia (Anapa) grew vines and traded wine; ancient presses have been excavated.

history.title: Cossack wines of the Don
history.text: Don Cossack stanitsas such as Tsimlyanskaya and Razdorskaya grew native red grapes; sparkling Tsimlyanskoye was praised by Pushkin.

history.title: Imperial Abrau-Durso
history.text: Tsar Alexander II founded an imperial estate at Abrau-Durso on 25 November 1870 to supply the court.

history.title: Golitsyn makes champagne for the tsar
history.text: Prince Lev Golitsyn, appointed head of the imperial vineyards, brought French winemakers to Abrau-Durso; by 1897 it held over 13,000 bottles of sparkling wine in its cellars.

history.title: Anti-alcohol campaign
history.text: Gorbachev's campaign uprooted vineyards across southern Russia.

history.title: Federal wine law
history.text: Law 468-FZ on viticulture and winemaking came into force on 26 June 2020, reserving 'Russian wine' for domestic grapes and setting up ZGU and ZNMP designations.

country.classification: Since the 2020 law, Russian wine can carry a protected geographical indication (ZGU, roughly an IGP: Kuban, Kuban. Taman Peninsula, Don Valley, Stavropol, Dagestan, Terek Valley, Lower Volga and others) or a protected designation of origin (ZNMP, smaller zones often tied to one estate, especially in Krasnodar Krai). 'Russian wine' requires 100 percent Russian-grown grapes; wine made from imported bulk or concentrate must say so. Russia also lists Crimea and Sevastopol as geographical indications, which Ukraine and most states regard as occupied Ukrainian territory.
country.climate_soils: Continental, with harsh winters in Rostov, Stavropol and Dagestan where vines are buried for protection; the Black Sea coast around Anapa, Taman and Novorossiysk is milder. Soils range from chernozem to marl, limestone and the sandy islands of the Don.

grapes.name: Krasnostop Zolotovsky
grapes.note: Don native red, deep and tannic, the rising star.

grapes.name: Tsimlyansky Cherny
grapes.note: Don red, the base of sparkling Tsimlyanskoye.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling

regions.name: Kuban (Krasnodar)
regions.tagline: The Black Sea coast and Taman peninsula: the heart of modern Russian wine.
regions.summary: Krasnodar Krai produces the largest share of Russian wine. Its zones include the Taman peninsula (Fanagoria, Kuban-Vino's Château Tamagne), Anapa (Gai-Kodzor, Château le Grand Vostock), the Abrau-Durso and Novorossiysk area, and Krymsk (Lefkadia).
regions.history: Greek Phanagoria and Gorgippia; imperial Abrau-Durso (1870).
regions.terroir: Sea-moderated, marl and limestone near Novorossiysk, sandy and chernozem soils on Taman.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Riesling, Aligoté, Krasnostop.
regions.classification: ZGU Kuban, Kuban. Taman Peninsula and many ZNMP.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025
Simple Wine News, How Russian wine laws are changing (2020)

regions.name: Don Valley
regions.summary: Rostov oblast's vineyards line the lower Don around Razdorskaya, Tsimlyansk and Starocherkassk. Native grapes such as Krasnostop Zolotovsky and Tsimlyansky Cherny are revived by Vedernikov, Kuban-Vino's Don estate and others.
regions.history: Cossack viticulture since the seventeenth century.
regions.terroir: Cold winters (vines buried), hot summers, sandy and chernozem soils.
regions.grapes: Krasnostop Zolotovsky, Tsimlyansky Cherny, Plechistik, Sibirkovy.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025
Simple Wine News, How Russian wine laws are changing (2020)

regions.name: Dagestan
regions.summary: Dagestan's Caspian lowlands around Derbent and Kizlyar grow table grapes, brandy grapes and increasingly wine grapes; the Derbent Wine Company planted about 1,400 hectares of new vineyards.
regions.history: Derbent's Sasanian citadel and its vines; Kizlyar brandy since the nineteenth century.

sources.title: OIV, State of the World Wine Sector in 2025
Simple Wine News, How Russian wine laws are changing (2020)

sites.name: Abrau-Durso
sites.text: The imperial estate founded in 1870 beside Lake Abrau near Novorossiysk, where Prince Lev Golitsyn and French winemakers made Russia's first traditional-method sparkling wine for the tsars; the Soviet 'Sovetskoye Shampanskoye' style was modelled on it. Its tunnels run into the hills above the lake.

sites.name: Phanagoria
sites.text: The largest Greek city on the Taman peninsula, founded around 543 BC, with ancient wine presses and amphora workshops; the modern Fanagoria winery takes its name.

sites.name: Gorgippia
sites.text: The Greek city of Gorgippia, founded in the sixth century BC under modern Anapa, part of the Bosporan Kingdom; its open-air museum includes ancient wine-making installations and amphorae, evidence of wine on this coast for over two thousand years.

sites.name: Lefkadia
sites.text: Estate in the Lefkadia valley near Moldavanskoye in the Krymsk district of Kuban, planted from 2006; it holds its own protected designation of origin.

sites.name: Gai-Kodzor
sites.text: Village in the hills behind Anapa, a few kilometres from the Black Sea, where several of Kuban's new estates, including Gai-Kodzor winery, planted marl and limestone slopes from the 2000s.

sites.name: Tsimlyansk
sites.text: Town on the Don whose Cossack winemakers made the famous sparkling red Tsimlyanskoye from the native Tsimlyansky Cherny, praised by Pushkin. The Don valley around it is now the centre of a revival of Cossack grape varieties.

sites.name: Razdorskaya
sites.text: Cossack stanitsa on the Don, centre of the native-grape revival and home of an ethnographic museum.
